title: LLM-based Multimodal Feedback Produces Equivalent Learning and Better Student Perceptions than Educator Feedback
venue: LAK 2026: 16th International Learning Analytics and Knowledge Conference
extended_summary:
This paper examines whether real-time LLM-based multimodal feedback can match or exceed educator-authored feedback in educational effectiveness and student experience. The core problem is that timely, targeted, and multimodal feedback is valuable for learning but difficult for instructors to provide at scale. The authors ask whether an AI system that combines structured textual feedback with retrieved course slides and optional AI audio narration can support learning as effectively as business-as-usual educator feedback while improving engagement and perceptions.

The intervention was an AI-facilitated multimodal feedback system embedded into an online learning workflow. After students answered multiple-choice and open-ended practice questions, the system generated structured corrective feedback using GPT-5, retrieved the most relevant lecture slide via retrieval-augmented generation, and offered optional streaming audio narration. This treatment was compared against a control condition in which learners received fixed, pre-written educator feedback and access to the same slide deck without targeted slide retrieval. The study used a randomized controlled online crowdsourcing experiment with pre-test, practice activities, post-test, and post-survey measures.

Participants were 197 U.S.-based university or college students recruited via Prolific, completing the study in a single online session hosted on Qualtrics. The learning content came from a learning sciences course on the multimedia principle in e-learning design. Learners completed 14 MCQs and 2 open-ended questions on the pre-test, 13 learning-by-doing activities with immediate feedback, and then the same post-test and a perception survey. The study also analyzed usage logs such as submissions, revisions, and time on task.

The main finding is that AI multimodal feedback produced learning gains equivalent to educator feedback: both groups improved significantly from pre- to post-test, and the between-group difference in post-test performance was not significant after controlling for pre-test scores. However, the AI condition was rated significantly better on mental effort, satisfaction, specificity, clarity, simplicity/conciseness, and motivation, while being comparable on correctness, trust, and acceptance. Log data suggested different engagement patterns by question type: educator feedback led to more MCQ retries, whereas AI feedback encouraged more revision behavior on open-ended items. The authors conclude that structured, context-aware AI multimodal feedback can be a scalable way to reduce instructor workload while maintaining learning outcomes and improving the learner experience.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A real-time LLM-based multimodal feedback system that generates structured textual corrective feedback, retrieves relevant slide pages via RAG, and provides optional AI audio narration grounded in course materials.
identified_tools.use_case: Studied as an AI-facilitated multimodal feedback intervention for university learners completing multiple-choice and open-ended learning-by-doing activities, compared against fixed educator-authored business-as-usual feedback in an online randomized experiment.

findings.finding_summary: In a randomized online crowdsourcing experiment, AI multimodal feedback produced significant pre-post learning gains within the treatment group (t=-5.6273, p<0.001, Cohen's d=0.7623), but did not outperform educator feedback after controlling for pre-test scores. ANCOVA showed no significant condition effect on post-test scores (F=0.91, p=0.34, partial η2=0.0047), indicating equivalent learning outcomes relative to educator feedback.
findings.measure: Pre-test to post-test knowledge scores on multimedia principle content; ANCOVA on post-test controlling for pre-test

findings.finding_summary: The AI system delivered feedback with median response time of 0.299 seconds for multiple-choice questions and 6.23 seconds for open-ended questions. Using word-count proxy estimates, the authors report the system was approximately 2.77× more time-efficient than authoring equivalent human text feedback (985/356 ≈ 2.77), suggesting reduced educator workload and rapid learner support.
findings.measure: System response time and estimated authoring efficiency relative to human-authored feedback
findings.effect_size: 2.77× more time-efficient; MCQ median=0.299s; OEQ median=6.23s

findings.finding_summary: Overall active-learning actions did not significantly differ between conditions (Mann–Whitney U=4075.5, p=0.0738). By question type, AI feedback was associated with fewer multiple-choice submissions than educator feedback (U=5660.5, p=0.02) and a trend toward more open-ended submissions (U=4060.5, p=0.066), consistent with less trial-and-error on MCQs and more iterative revision on OEQs.
findings.measure: Usage-log active learning actions (submit/update counts) overall and by question type
findings.effect_size: U=4075.5 overall; U=5660.5 MCQ; U=4060.5 OEQ

findings.finding_summary: Total time spent on learning-by-doing activities did not significantly differ between AI and educator-feedback conditions. The business-as-usual group spent a median of 21.13 minutes and the AI group a median of 25.44 minutes, with an independent-samples t-test showing no significant difference (t=-0.413, p=0.680, Cohen's d=-0.062).

Learners reported significantly lower mental effort and higher satisfaction with AI multimodal feedback than with educator feedback. Mental effort ratings were 6.17 vs. 7.22 (U=5190.50, p=0.0006), and satisfaction ratings were 4.46 vs. 4.19 (U=3310.50, p=0.0240), favoring the AI condition.
findings.measure: Post-survey ratings of mental effort and satisfaction

findings.finding_summary: Participants rated AI feedback significantly higher on specificity, clarity, simplicity, and motivation than educator feedback. Survey results were specificity 4.28 vs. 3.78 (U=2638.00, p=0.0001), clarity 4.68 vs. 4.48 (U=3346.50, p=0.0199), simplicity 4.09 vs. 3.75 (U=3246.00, p=0.0207), and motivation 4.04 vs. 3.70 (U=3174.50, p=0.0146).
findings.measure: Post-survey ratings of feedback specificity, clarity, simplicity, and motivation

findings.finding_summary: Perceived correctness, trust, and acceptance of AI feedback were statistically comparable to educator feedback. Reported tests were correctness U=3806.50, p=0.5378; trust U=3543.00, p=0.1456; and acceptance U=3614.00, p=0.2393, indicating no significant differences on these dimensions.
findings.measure: Post-survey ratings of correctness, trust, and acceptance

quality_tier_rationale: This is a randomized controlled online experiment with a comparison condition and n=197, which is stronger than correlational evidence. However, it was conducted in a short-term crowdsourcing setting rather than an authentic classroom, and the main between-group academic outcome was equivalence/null rather than a clear treatment advantage.
impact_tier_rationale: Academic impact was unclear between groups because post-test differences were not significant (F=0.91, p=0.34, partial η2=0.0047), despite positive within-group gains. The intervention showed positive perception and efficiency benefits, but core learning impact relative to educator feedback was modest/unclear.
